Chapter 2: Creating a Home Where Questions and Doubts Are Welcome.
Let’s dive into something that every family exploring faith will recognize—questions and doubts. If you’ve ever heard your child ask, “Why do we believe this?” or “How come we go to church?”—you’re not alone. As kids grow, it’s completely natural for them to start wondering about their beliefs and the world around them. But here’s the thing: instead of seeing these questions as a problem, what if we treated them like opportunities?
Think about it—uncertainty isn’t a threat to faith; it’s actually a normal part of the journey. Just like a toddler learns to walk by stumbling, we all grow stronger in our beliefs by wrestling with tough questions. It’s not a sign of weak faith, but proof that someone’s really thinking and engaging.
A lot of families feel the urge to steer clear of tricky topics, or they might give easy answers just to move on. But have you ever noticed how that can leave kids feeling frustrated or disconnected? Curious minds need space to explore. So, creating a home where it’s safe to ask anything—whether it’s about God, church traditions, or even doubts themselves—can make all the difference.
One of the best ways to encourage this openness is by modeling curiosity and humility yourself. Imagine saying, “I’m not sure, but let’s find out together.” That simple phrase shows that faith isn’t about having all the answers. It’s about searching for truth as a family. And it teaches kids that it’s okay to grow, to change your mind, and to keep learning.
Here are a few practical ways you can encourage open conversations about faith at home:
First, set aside regular times for discussion. Maybe it’s at the dinner table, right before bed, or even during drives to school—any time when everyone’s relaxed and together works well.
Second, practice listening without judgment. Let your kids express their doubts and disagreements without worrying that you’ll be upset or disappointed.
Third, share your own experiences. Talk about the questions you’ve faced, the struggles you’ve had, and how your faith has evolved over time.
And finally, explore resources together. That might mean reading a thought-provoking book, watching a documentary, or attending events that tackle big questions about Christianity.
For example, if your child asks, “Why do bad things happen in the world?”—instead of jumping to a quick answer, you might respond, “That’s a really important question. People have wondered about that for a long time. Let’s talk about what we think, and maybe check out what others have said, too.” By doing this, you’re showing your child that their curiosity matters, and that it’s okay not to have everything figured out right away.
When we normalize questions and doubts, we help prevent the silent skepticism that can quietly push kids away from faith as they get older. Instead, they see that faith is strong enough to handle tough questions—and that their ideas and voices count.
This kind of openness doesn’t just help inside the home. It also gets your family ready for a world filled with different beliefs and perspectives. When kids learn to ask questions at home, they grow into adults who can talk with empathy and confidence—even when they don’t agree with everyone around them.
So, the real goal here isn’t just about faith. It’s about building trust, respect, and a lifelong habit of thoughtful reflection. That’s the foundation you’ll need for the next step: living out those beliefs in your everyday actions and values.
